subject: Biology

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by water.
solution: Water is polar because oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen, producing partial charges.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in water.
solution: Hydrogen bonds form between water molecules; individually weak bonds collectively produce cohesion, high specific heat capacity and strong solvent properties.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to water.
solution: The bent shape and unequal charge distribution of a water molecule allow each molecule to form multiple hydrogen bonds.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of water to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Evaporation removes the fastest water molecules and therefore cools a leaf or sweating animal.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure the cooling of wet and dry model surfaces under identical airflow. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: surface moisture condition.
Dependent variable: change in surface temperature.
Controlled variable: initial temperature and airflow.
Expected trend: the wet surface should cool more because evaporation removes latent heat.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss water across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Water is polar because oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen, producing partial charges. (2) Hydrogen bonds form between water molecules; individually weak bonds collectively produce cohesion, high specific heat capacity and strong solvent properties. (3) The bent shape and unequal charge distribution of a water molecule allow each molecule to form multiple hydrogen bonds. (4) Evaporation removes the fastest water molecules and therefore cools a leaf or sweating animal. (5) Relate water's molecular polarity and hydrogen bonding to transport, temperature stability and habitat conditions in living systems.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by nucleic acids.
solution: DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides, each containing a pentose sugar, phosphate group and nitrogenous base.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in nucleic acids.
solution: Nucleotides join by condensation reactions that form phosphodiester bonds; complementary bases associate by hydrogen bonding.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to nucleic acids.
solution: Antiparallel DNA strands and specific base pairing allow stable information storage and accurate copying.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of nucleic acids to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: A base sequence can store information because the order of four bases can vary enormously along a polynucleotide.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare nuclease digestion of DNA at different enzyme concentrations. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: nuclease concentration.
Dependent variable: amount of intact DNA remaining.
Controlled variable: initial DNA concentration and incubation time.
Expected trend: more nuclease should leave less intact DNA until substrate becomes limiting.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss nucleic acids across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides, each containing a pentose sugar, phosphate group and nitrogenous base. (2) Nucleotides join by condensation reactions that form phosphodiester bonds; complementary bases associate by hydrogen bonding. (3) Antiparallel DNA strands and specific base pairing allow stable information storage and accurate copying. (4) A base sequence can store information because the order of four bases can vary enormously along a polynucleotide. (5) Explain how nucleotide structure, base sequence and complementary pairing support both heredity and gene expression.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by cell structure.
solution: Cells share a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, genetic material and ribosomes, while prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ in compartmentalization.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in cell structure.
solution: Electron microscopy resolves ultrastructure at shorter wavelengths than light microscopy, but preparation can introduce artefacts.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to cell structure.
solution: A high surface-area-to-volume ratio shortens diffusion distances and increases exchange capacity relative to metabolic demand.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of cell structure to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Magnification equals image size divided by actual size, with all measurements converted to the same unit.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will estimate cell size from calibrated micrographs at several magnifications. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: microscope magnification.
Dependent variable: measured image size and calculated actual size.
Controlled variable: the same specimen and scale calibration.
Expected trend: image size increases with magnification while calculated actual size should remain constant.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss cell structure across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Cells share a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, genetic material and ribosomes, while prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ in compartmentalization. (2) Electron microscopy resolves ultrastructure at shorter wavelengths than light microscopy, but preparation can introduce artefacts. (3) A high surface-area-to-volume ratio shortens diffusion distances and increases exchange capacity relative to metabolic demand. (4) Magnification equals image size divided by actual size, with all measurements converted to the same unit. (5) Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and explain how microscopy and scale influence the evidence available to biologists.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by diversity of organisms.
solution: Biological diversity includes variation in genes, species and ecosystems, and can be described using shared and distinguishing traits.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in diversity of organisms.
solution: Dichotomous keys identify organisms through a sequence of paired, mutually exclusive observable choices.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to diversity of organisms.
solution: Diagnostic morphological or molecular characteristics allow organisms to be grouped while acknowledging variation within groups.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of diversity of organisms to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Molecular sequence evidence can reveal relationships that convergent external features may obscure.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will test the reliability of a dichotomous key using independently identified specimens. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: specimen presented.
Dependent variable: proportion identified correctly.
Controlled variable: observer training and key version.
Expected trend: accuracy should be highest when diagnostic features are unambiguous and consistently observed.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss diversity of organisms across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution:

Diagnostic morphological or molecular characteristics allow organisms to be grouped while acknowledging variation within groups. (4) Molecular sequence evidence can reveal relationships that convergent external features may obscure. (5) Explain how classification systems organize biodiversity while new evidence can change the boundaries or relationships of groups.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by evolution and speciation.
solution: Evolution is a change in heritable characteristics of a population across generations.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in evolution and speciation.
solution: Reproductive isolation limits gene flow; mutation, selection and drift can then cause populations to diverge until they form separate species.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to evolution and speciation.
solution: Homologous structures share an underlying origin even when natural selection has modified them for different functions.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of evolution and speciation to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Geographical isolation can initiate allopatric speciation when separated populations experience different selection pressures.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare allele frequencies in replicate populations exposed to different environments. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: environmental condition.
Dependent variable: allele frequency over generations.
Controlled variable: starting allele frequency and population size.
Expected trend: alleles that increase reproductive success in an environment should tend to rise in frequency.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss evolution and speciation across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Evolution is a change in heritable characteristics of a population across generations. (3) Homologous structures share an underlying origin even when natural selection has modified them for different functions. (4) Geographical isolation can initiate allopatric speciation when separated populations experience different selection pressures. (5) Explain how multiple lines of evidence support evolution and how reduced gene flow can lead from variation within populations to speciation.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by conservation of biodiversity.
solution: Biodiversity conservation aims to maintain genetic, species and ecosystem diversity and the processes that sustain them.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in conservation of biodiversity.
solution: Habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution and climate change can reduce population size and increase extinction risk.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to conservation of biodiversity.
solution: Wildlife corridors connect habitat fragments, increasing movement and gene flow between otherwise isolated populations.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of conservation of biodiversity to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: In situ conservation preserves species in their ecological context, whereas ex situ methods maintain organisms or germplasm elsewhere.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will survey species richness in restored plots and matched unrestored plots. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: restoration treatment.
Dependent variable: species richness or diversity index.
Controlled variable: plot area and sampling effort.
Expected trend: effective restoration should increase richness over time relative to controls.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss conservation of biodiversity across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Biodiversity conservation aims to maintain genetic, species and ecosystem diversity and the processes that sustain them. (4) In situ conservation preserves species in their ecological context, whereas ex situ methods maintain organisms or germplasm elsewhere. (5) Evaluate conservation strategies using ecological effectiveness, genetic consequences, cost, ethics and local community needs.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by carbohydrates and lipids.
solution: Monosaccharides form larger carbohydrates, while fatty acids and glycerol form many lipids; both groups have energy and structural roles.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in carbohydrates and lipids.
solution: Condensation joins monomers while releasing water, and hydrolysis uses water to split larger molecules.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to carbohydrates and lipids.
solution: Phospholipids are amphipathic, with hydrophilic phosphate heads and hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of carbohydrates and lipids to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Triglycerides store more energy per unit mass than carbohydrates because their carbon atoms are more reduced.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare reducing-sugar test colour after hydrolysing different carbohydrate samples. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: carbohydrate sample.
Dependent variable: colour intensity or absorbance.
Controlled variable: sample volume and heating time.
Expected trend: samples yielding more reducing sugars after hydrolysis should give a stronger positive test.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss carbohydrates and lipids across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution:

Phospholipids are amphipathic, with hydrophilic phosphate heads and hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails. (4) Triglycerides store more energy per unit mass than carbohydrates because their carbon atoms are more reduced. (5) Relate the structures of monosaccharides, polysaccharides, triglycerides and phospholipids to their biological functions.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by proteins.
solution: Proteins are chains of amino acids whose sequences determine folding and biological function.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in proteins.
solution: Peptide bonds form by condensation; interactions among R groups drive secondary, tertiary and sometimes quaternary structure.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to proteins.
solution: Globular proteins often have specific binding sites, whereas fibrous proteins commonly provide tensile or structural support.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of proteins to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: A change in one amino acid can alter folding, stability or binding and therefore change phenotype.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure protein denaturation across a range of temperatures. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: temperature.
Dependent variable: solubility or retained biological activity.
Controlled variable: protein concentration and exposure time.
Expected trend: activity should decline beyond the temperature range that preserves native folding.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss proteins across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Proteins are chains of amino acids whose sequences determine folding and biological function. questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by membranes and membrane transport.
solution: Cell membranes are fluid phospholipid bilayers containing proteins, cholesterol and carbohydrates.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in membranes and membrane transport.
solution: Simple diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient; active transport uses energy to move substances against a gradient.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to membranes and membrane transport.
solution: Hydrophobic bilayer interiors restrict ions and polar molecules, while channel and carrier proteins provide selective routes.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of membranes and membrane transport to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Increasing extracellular solute concentration can cause an animal cell to lose water by osmosis and shrink.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure pigment leakage from beetroot tissue after exposure to different temperatures. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: temperature.
Dependent variable: pigment absorbance of surrounding solution.
Controlled variable: disc size and exposure time.
Expected trend: higher temperatures should increase leakage as membrane integrity is disrupted.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss membranes and membrane transport across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Cell membranes are fluid phospholipid bilayers containing proteins, cholesterol and carbohydrates. (2) Simple diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient; active transport uses energy to move substances against a gradient. (4) Increasing extracellular solute concentration can cause an animal cell to lose water by osmosis and shrink. (5) Compare transport mechanisms and explain how membrane composition creates selective permeability and dynamic cell boundaries.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by organelles and compartmentalization.
solution: Eukaryotic organelles compartmentalize reactions, allowing distinct conditions and processes to occur efficiently within one cell.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in organelles and compartmentalization.
solution: Proteins for secretion are translated at rough ER, modified in ER and Golgi, and transported in vesicles to the plasma membrane.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to organelles and compartmentalization.
solution: Cristae increase inner mitochondrial membrane area for electron transport and ATP synthesis.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of organelles and compartmentalization to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Cells with high rates of protein secretion usually contain abundant rough ER and Golgi apparatus.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare organelle abundance in micrographs of cells with different functions. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: cell type.
Dependent variable: relative area or number of a selected organelle.
Controlled variable: magnification and sampling method.
Expected trend: organelle abundance should correspond to the dominant metabolic function of each cell type.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss organelles and compartmentalization across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Eukaryotic organelles compartmentalize reactions, allowing distinct conditions and processes to occur efficiently within one cell. (5) Explain how compartmentalization coordinates synthesis, transport, energy conversion and degradation in eukaryotic cells.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by cell specialization.
solution: Specialized cells express particular genes and develop structures suited to their functions.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in cell specialization.
solution: Differential gene expression produces different proteins in cells that contain essentially the same genome.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to cell specialization.
solution: A root hair cell has a long projection that increases surface area for absorption of water and mineral ions.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of cell specialization to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Loss of specialization is often required before differentiated cells can contribute to tissue regeneration.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare uptake rates in cells with different surface-area-to-volume ratios. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: cell geometry or size.
Dependent variable: uptake rate per unit volume.
Controlled variable: external concentration and temperature.
Expected trend: cells with greater surface area relative to volume should show faster exchange per unit volume.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss cell specialization across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Specialized cells express particular genes and develop structures suited to their functions. questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by gas exchange.
solution: Gas-exchange surfaces maintain steep diffusion gradients and provide large, thin, moist areas for exchange.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in gas exchange.
solution: Ventilation refreshes the external medium and blood flow removes absorbed oxygen, maintaining concentration gradients.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to gas exchange.
solution: Alveoli have thin walls, extensive capillaries and a large collective surface area for rapid diffusion.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of gas exchange to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: During exercise, ventilation rate and cardiac output rise to support increased oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide removal.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure ventilation rate before and after standardized exercise. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: exercise intensity.
Dependent variable: ventilation rate.
Controlled variable: exercise duration and participant posture.
Expected trend: ventilation rate should increase as metabolic demand and carbon dioxide production rise.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss gas exchange across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by transport.
solution: Multicellular organisms use mass transport systems because diffusion alone is too slow across large distances.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in transport.
solution: Pressure differences drive bulk flow: the heart generates blood pressure and transpiration helps pull xylem sap upward.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to transport.
solution: Arteries have strong elastic walls for high pressure, while capillaries have thin walls for exchange.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of transport to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Closing stomata reduces water loss but can also reduce carbon dioxide uptake and photosynthesis.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure transpiration under different wind speeds using a potometer. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: wind speed.
Dependent variable: rate of bubble movement or water uptake.
Controlled variable: leaf area and light intensity.
Expected trend: moderate wind should increase water uptake by reducing the humid boundary layer.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss transport across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by adaptation to environment.
solution: An adaptation is a heritable characteristic that increases survival or reproductive success in a particular environment.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in adaptation to environment.
solution: Environmental conditions act as selection pressures on existing variation rather than directly producing needed traits.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to adaptation to environment.
solution: Thick waxy cuticles and reduced leaves can reduce water loss in terrestrial plants.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of adaptation to environment to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: A characteristic advantageous in one environment may carry a cost or become disadvantageous in another.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare water loss from leaves with different cuticle thicknesses. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: cuticle thickness or leaf type.
Dependent variable: mass of water lost per unit area.
Controlled variable: temperature and airflow.
Expected trend: thicker cuticles should be associated with lower water loss under dry conditions.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss adaptation to environment across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) An adaptation is a heritable characteristic that increases survival or reproductive success in a particular environment. questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by ecological niches.
solution: A species' ecological niche includes the resources it uses, conditions it tolerates and interactions it has with other organisms.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in ecological niches.
solution: Competition occurs when organisms require the same limiting resource; niche differentiation can reduce overlap and permit coexistence.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to ecological niches.
solution: Fundamental niche describes potential conditions without biotic constraints, while realized niche reflects actual occupancy.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of ecological niches to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Removing a competitor can allow a species to occupy a broader part of its fundamental niche.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure resource use by two species when grown alone and together. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: presence of the competing species.
Dependent variable: range or amount of resource use.
Controlled variable: resource supply and habitat area.
Expected trend: competition should reduce or shift resource use when the species occur together.

questions.label: Hard

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by enzymes and metabolism.
solution: Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower activation energy without being consumed by the reaction.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in enzymes and metabolism.
solution: Substrate binding stabilizes a transition state; rate depends on collisions, active-site compatibility and environmental conditions.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to enzymes and metabolism.
solution: An enzyme's three-dimensional active site gives substrate specificity while allowing induced fit during binding.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of enzymes and metabolism to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: A competitive inhibitor reduces rate by occupying the active site, an effect that can be partly overcome by increasing substrate concentration.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure enzyme rate at different substrate concentrations. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: substrate concentration.
Dependent variable: initial reaction rate.
Controlled variable: enzyme concentration and temperature.
Expected trend: rate should rise and then plateau as active sites become saturated.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss enzymes and metabolism across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by cell respiration.
solution: Cell respiration transfers chemical energy from organic molecules into ATP that can power cellular work.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in cell respiration.
solution: Glycolysis splits glucose and yields a small amount of ATP; aerobic pathways use oxygen-linked electron transport to produce much more ATP.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to cell respiration.
solution: The inner mitochondrial membrane holds electron carriers and ATP synthase, while the matrix contains enzymes for carbon oxidation.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of cell respiration to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: When oxygen is unavailable, fermentation regenerates NAD so glycolysis can continue, but ATP yield remains low.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure respiration rate of germinating seeds at different temperatures. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: temperature.
Dependent variable: oxygen consumption or carbon dioxide production.
Controlled variable: seed mass and germination stage.
Expected trend: rate should increase to an optimum and then fall if enzymes or membranes are disrupted.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by photosynthesis.
solution: Photosynthesis uses light energy to synthesize organic compounds from carbon dioxide and water.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in photosynthesis.
solution: Light-dependent reactions produce ATP and reduced carriers; carbon fixation uses these products to build carbohydrates.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to photosynthesis.
solution: Thylakoid membranes organize pigments, electron carriers and ATP synthase, while carbon fixation occurs in the stroma.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of photosynthesis to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: At low light intensity, increasing light can increase photosynthetic rate until another factor becomes limiting.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure oxygen production by aquatic plants across light intensities. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: light intensity.
Dependent variable: oxygen production rate.
Controlled variable: temperature and carbon dioxide availability.
Expected trend: oxygen production should rise and then level off as another factor becomes limiting.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by neural signalling.
solution: Neurons transmit information electrically along membranes and chemically across many synapses.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in neural signalling.
solution: Depolarization opens voltage-gated sodium channels; subsequent potassium movement helps repolarize the membrane.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to neural signalling.
solution: Myelin insulates axons and enables saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of neural signalling to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: A neurotransmitter can be excitatory or inhibitory depending on the receptor and ion channels in the postsynaptic cell.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure conduction speed in axons with different diameters. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: axon diameter.
Dependent variable: conduction speed.
Controlled variable: temperature and myelination state.
Expected trend: larger diameter should generally increase conduction speed by reducing internal resistance.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss neural signalling across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Neurons transmit information electrically along membranes and chemically across many synapses. (2) Depolarization opens voltage-gated sodium channels; subsequent potassium movement helps repolarize the membrane. (3) Myelin insulates axons and enables saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier. (4) A neurotransmitter can be excitatory or inhibitory depending on the receptor and ion channels in the postsynaptic cell. (5) Explain how membrane potentials, ion channels, myelin and synapses allow rapid yet modifiable communication.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by integration of body systems.
solution: Body systems interact to maintain internal conditions and supply cells with materials while removing wastes.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in integration of body systems.
solution: Receptors detect change, coordinating centres process information and effectors produce responses through feedback pathways.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to integration of body systems.
solution: Dense capillary networks link transport with exchange at lungs, intestines, kidneys and active tissues.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of integration of body systems to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Exercise simultaneously alters ventilation, circulation, metabolism and thermoregulation rather than affecting one isolated system.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure heart rate and ventilation during graded exercise. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: exercise workload.
Dependent variable: heart rate and ventilation rate.
Controlled variable: exercise duration and participant fitness.
Expected trend: both responses should rise with workload to support increased cellular respiration.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss integration of body systems across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Body systems interact to maintain internal conditions and supply cells with materials while removing wastes. (2) Receptors detect change, coordinating centres process information and effectors produce responses through feedback pathways. (3) Dense capillary networks link transport with exchange at lungs, intestines, kidneys and active tissues. (4) Exercise simultaneously alters ventilation, circulation, metabolism and thermoregulation rather than affecting one isolated system. (5) Explain how nervous, endocrine, circulatory, respiratory and excretory systems coordinate during a physiological challenge.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by defence against disease.
solution: Defence includes physical barriers, innate responses and specific adaptive immunity.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in defence against disease.
solution: Clonal selection activates lymphocytes with receptors complementary to an antigen, producing effector and memory cells.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to defence against disease.
solution: Antibodies have variable binding regions and constant regions that help eliminate bound targets.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of defence against disease to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Vaccination exposes the immune system to antigen without causing the full disease, promoting memory-cell formation.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare antibody concentration after primary and booster vaccination. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: vaccination exposure number.
Dependent variable: antibody concentration over time.
Controlled variable: vaccine dose and sampling interval.
Expected trend: a booster should produce a faster and larger secondary response because memory cells are present.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss defence against disease across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Defence includes physical barriers, innate responses and specific adaptive immunity. (2) Clonal selection activates lymphocytes with receptors complementary to an antigen, producing effector and memory cells. (3) Antibodies have variable binding regions and constant regions that help eliminate bound targets. (4) Vaccination exposes the immune system to antigen without causing the full disease, promoting memory-cell formation. (5) Compare innate and adaptive defence and explain specificity, memory, vaccination and limits such as antigenic change.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by populations and communities.
solution: A population consists of members of one species in an area, while a community includes interacting populations of different species.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in populations and communities.
solution: Density-dependent factors intensify with population density and can contribute to logistic growth around carrying capacity.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to populations and communities.
solution: Random quadrats estimate abundance of relatively immobile organisms while reducing placement bias.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of populations and communities to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: A predator decline may allow prey abundance to increase, but food limitation and disease can modify the response.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will estimate plant density using increasing numbers of randomly placed quadrats. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: number of quadrats.
Dependent variable: estimated mean density and uncertainty.
Controlled variable: quadrat size and habitat area.
Expected trend: the estimate should become more stable and uncertainty should usually decrease as sample size rises.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss populations and communities across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) A population consists of members of one species in an area, while a community includes interacting populations of different species. (2) Density-dependent factors intensify with population density and can contribute to logistic growth around carrying capacity. (3) Random quadrats estimate abundance of relatively immobile organisms while reducing placement bias. (4) A predator decline may allow prey abundance to increase, but food limitation and disease can modify the response. (5) Explain how sampling, competition, predation, disease and carrying capacity shape population and community patterns.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by transfers of energy and matter.
solution: Energy flows through ecosystems and is dissipated as heat, whereas chemical elements are recycled.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in transfers of energy and matter.
solution: Only part of the energy in one trophic level becomes biomass available to the next because of respiration, waste and uneaten material.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to transfers of energy and matter.
solution: Food webs show multiple feeding relationships and therefore represent ecosystems more realistically than single chains.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of transfers of energy and matter to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Removing a top predator can cause indirect changes across several trophic levels.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure biomass at successive trophic levels in comparable ecosystems. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: trophic level.
Dependent variable: dry biomass or energy content.
Controlled variable: sample area and season.
Expected trend: available biomass and energy should generally decline at higher trophic levels.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss transfers of energy and matter across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Energy flows through ecosystems and is dissipated as heat, whereas chemical elements are recycled. (2) Only part of the energy in one trophic level becomes biomass available to the next because of respiration, waste and uneaten material. (3) Food webs show multiple feeding relationships and therefore represent ecosystems more realistically than single chains. (4) Removing a top predator can cause indirect changes across several trophic levels. (5) Trace energy and carbon through producers, consumers, decomposers and the abiotic environment, including human disruption.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by dna replication.
solution: DNA replication is semi-conservative: each daughter molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in dna replication.
solution: Helicase separates strands, DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction and ligase joins fragments.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to dna replication.
solution: Antiparallel strands require continuous synthesis on one template and discontinuous synthesis on the other.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of dna replication to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Complementary base pairing allows each parental strand to act as a template for accurate copying.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure incorporation of labelled nucleotides during S phase. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: time after label addition.
Dependent variable: label incorporated into DNA.
Controlled variable: cell number and nucleotide concentration.
Expected trend: incorporation should rise while DNA synthesis is active and stop when replication is complete.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss dna replication across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution:
A strong response should: (1) DNA replication is semi-conservative: each daughter molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand. (2) Helicase separates strands,
DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction and ligase joins fragments. (3) Antiparallel strands require continuous synthesis on one template and discontinuous synthesis on the other. (4) Complementary base pairing allows each parental strand to act as a template for accurate copying. (5) Explain how enzyme action, strand polarity, proofreading and complementary pairing produce rapid and accurate replication.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by protein synthesis.
solution: Protein synthesis converts nucleotide sequence information into an amino-acid sequence through transcription and translation.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in protein synthesis.
solution: RNA polymerase makes RNA from a DNA template; ribosomes read mRNA codons while tRNAs deliver corresponding amino acids.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to protein synthesis.
solution: A ribosome positions mRNA and tRNAs so peptide bonds form in the codon-defined sequence.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of protein synthesis to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Because the genetic code is degenerate, some base substitutions do not change the encoded amino acid.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure protein production after altering mRNA concentration. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: mRNA concentration.
Dependent variable: protein produced per unit time.
Controlled variable: ribosome concentration and amino-acid supply.
Expected trend: protein production should rise until another translation component becomes limiting.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss protein synthesis across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution:
A strong response should: (1) Protein synthesis converts nucleotide sequence information into an amino-acid sequence through transcription and translation. (2) RNA polymerase makes RNA from a DNA template; ribosomes read mRNA codons while tRNAs deliver corresponding amino acids. (3) A ribosome positions mRNA and tRNAs so peptide bonds form in the codon-defined sequence. (4)
Because the genetic code is degenerate, some base substitutions do not change the encoded amino acid. (5) Trace information from DNA to functional protein and explain the roles of base pairing, codons, tRNA and ribosomes.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by mutations and gene editing.
solution: A mutation is a change in genetic material and can be neutral, harmful or beneficial depending on context.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in mutations and gene editing.
solution: Substitution, insertion and deletion can alter coding or regulatory sequences; insertions and deletions may shift the reading frame.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to mutations and gene editing.
solution: CRISPR systems use sequence complementarity to target a nuclease to a selected DNA region.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of mutations and gene editing to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Editing a somatic cell affects the treated individual, whereas germline editing could be inherited and raises broader ethical concerns.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure mutation frequency after different doses of ultraviolet radiation. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: ultraviolet dose.
Dependent variable: mutation frequency.
Controlled variable: cell type and post-exposure growth time.
Expected trend: mutation frequency should generally increase with dose because more DNA damage is produced.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss mutations and gene editing across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) A mutation is a change in genetic material and can be neutral, harmful or beneficial depending on context. (2) Substitution, insertion and deletion can alter coding or regulatory sequences; insertions and deletions may shift the reading frame. (3) CRISPR systems use sequence complementarity to target a nuclease to a selected DNA region. (4) Editing a somatic cell affects the treated individual, whereas germline editing could be inherited and raises broader ethical concerns. (5) Evaluate benefits, risks, limitations and ethical issues of gene editing for research, medicine and ecosystems.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by cell and nuclear division.
solution: The cell cycle coordinates growth, DNA replication and division, with checkpoints reducing transmission of damaged genomes.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in cell and nuclear division.
solution: Mitosis separates sister chromatids to produce genetically similar nuclei, while cytokinesis divides the cell.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to cell and nuclear division.
solution: Chromosome condensation and spindle attachment allow replicated DNA molecules to be moved accurately.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of cell and nuclear division to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Loss of cell-cycle regulation can permit uncontrolled division and contribute to tumour formation.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will calculate mitotic index in tissues exposed to different treatments. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: treatment.
Dependent variable: proportion of cells in mitosis.
Controlled variable: tissue region and counting method.
Expected trend: a treatment that stimulates division should raise mitotic index relative to the control.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss cell and nuclear division across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution:
A strong response should: (1) The cell cycle coordinates growth, DNA replication and division, with checkpoints reducing transmission of damaged genomes. (2) Mitosis separates sister chromatids to produce genetically similar nuclei, while cytokinesis divides the cell. (3) Chromosome condensation and spindle attachment allow replicated DNA molecules to be moved accurately. (4) Loss of cell-cycle regulation can permit uncontrolled division and contribute to tumour formation. (5)
Explain chromosome behaviour through the cell cycle and relate checkpoints, stem cells and uncontrolled division to organism function.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by water potential.
solution: Water moves by osmosis from higher water potential to lower water potential across a selectively permeable membrane.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in water potential.
solution: Adding solute lowers solute potential, while pressure can raise the total water potential of a plant cell.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to water potential.
solution: A rigid cell wall limits expansion and allows turgor pressure to develop without lysis.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of water potential to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: A plant cell placed in a sufficiently hypertonic solution loses water and may plasmolyse.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure mass change of plant tissue across sucrose concentrations. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: sucrose concentration.
Dependent variable: percentage mass change.
Controlled variable: tissue dimensions and immersion time.
Expected trend: mass change should become more negative as external water potential decreases.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss water potential across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Water moves by osmosis from higher water potential to lower water potential across a selectively permeable membrane. (2) Adding solute lowers solute potential, while pressure can raise the total water potential of a plant cell. (3) A rigid cell wall limits expansion and allows turgor pressure to develop without lysis. (4) A plant cell placed in a sufficiently hypertonic solution loses water and may plasmolyse. (5) Explain osmosis in plant and animal cells using water potential, solute concentration, pressure and membrane permeability.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by reproduction.
solution: Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two gametes, while asexual reproduction can produce genetically similar offspring rapidly.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in reproduction.
solution: Meiosis generates haploid gametes and variation through independent assortment and crossing over; fertilization restores diploidy.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to reproduction.
solution: Gametes are specialized for fusion and transfer of genetic material, with adaptations differing among organisms.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of reproduction to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Sexual reproduction can increase variation but requires more time and energy than many asexual strategies.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare seed set under different pollination treatments. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: pollination treatment.
Dependent variable: number or proportion of seeds formed.
Controlled variable: flower age and plant genotype.
Expected trend: treatments that successfully transfer compatible pollen should produce greater seed set.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss reproduction across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two gametes, while asexual reproduction can produce genetically similar offspring rapidly. (2) Meiosis generates haploid gametes and variation through independent assortment and crossing over; fertilization restores diploidy. (3) Gametes are specialized for fusion and transfer of genetic material, with adaptations differing among organisms. (4) Sexual reproduction can increase variation but requires more time and energy than many asexual strategies. (5) Compare reproductive strategies and explain how meiosis, gamete specialization, fertilization and parental investment affect success.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by inheritance.
solution: Alleles are alternative forms of a gene, and genotype contributes to phenotype together with environmental influences.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in inheritance.
solution: Alleles segregate during meiosis and combine at fertilization, allowing probabilities of offspring genotypes to be predicted.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to inheritance.
solution: Pedigrees display relationships and phenotypes across generations and can suggest modes of inheritance.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of inheritance to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: A test cross with a homozygous recessive individual can reveal the genotype of an organism with a dominant phenotype.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare observed offspring ratios with ratios predicted by a genetic model. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: parental cross.
Dependent variable: offspring phenotype counts.
Controlled variable: scoring criteria and sample size.
Expected trend: large samples should approach the predicted probabilities if the model assumptions are valid.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss inheritance across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Alleles are alternative forms of a gene, and genotype contributes to phenotype together with environmental influences. (2) Alleles segregate during meiosis and combine at fertilization, allowing probabilities of offspring genotypes to be predicted. (3) Pedigrees display relationships and phenotypes across generations and can suggest modes of inheritance. (4) A test cross with a homozygous recessive individual can reveal the genotype of an organism with a dominant phenotype. (5) Use meiosis, probability, pedigrees and molecular evidence to explain inheritance patterns beyond simple dominance.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by homeostasis.
solution: Homeostasis maintains internal variables within tolerable ranges through coordinated monitoring and response.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in homeostasis.
solution: Negative feedback opposes deviation from a set range, while positive feedback amplifies a process toward a defined endpoint.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to homeostasis.
solution: Receptors, control centres and effectors form pathways that adjust physiology when conditions change.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of homeostasis to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, lowering blood glucose toward its normal range.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure blood glucose response to meals with different carbohydrate compositions. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: meal composition.
Dependent variable: blood glucose concentration over time.
Controlled variable: fasting duration and meal energy.
Expected trend: rapidly absorbed carbohydrate should cause a faster and often larger glucose rise.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss homeostasis across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Homeostasis maintains internal variables within tolerable ranges through coordinated monitoring and response. (2) Negative feedback opposes deviation from a set range, while positive feedback amplifies a process toward a defined endpoint. (3) Receptors, control centres and effectors form pathways that adjust physiology when conditions change. (4) After a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, lowering blood glucose toward its normal range. (5) Compare regulation of temperature, blood glucose and water balance, including failures of feedback and interactions between systems.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by natural selection.
solution: Natural selection changes allele frequencies when heritable variation causes differences in survival or reproductive success.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in natural selection.
solution: Variation arises before selection; individuals with advantageous phenotypes contribute proportionally more alleles to later generations.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to natural selection.
solution: Heritable traits require a genetic basis, whereas acquired changes without genetic transmission do not drive evolutionary change.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of natural selection to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Antibiotic use selects for pre-existing resistant bacteria; it does not cause bacteria to mutate intentionally.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will track resistant-allele frequency under different antibiotic concentrations. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: antibiotic concentration.
Dependent variable: frequency of resistant survivors.
Controlled variable: starting population and exposure time.
Expected trend: resistant types should form a larger proportion of survivors as selection pressure increases.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss natural selection across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Natural selection changes allele frequencies when heritable variation causes differences in survival or reproductive success. (2) Variation arises before selection; individuals with advantageous phenotypes contribute proportionally more alleles to later generations. (3) Heritable traits require a genetic basis, whereas acquired changes without genetic transmission do not drive evolutionary change. (4) Antibiotic use selects for pre-existing resistant bacteria; it does not cause bacteria to mutate intentionally. (5) Explain natural selection from variation to allele-frequency change and apply it to resistance, artificial selection and changing environments.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by stability and change.
solution: Ecosystems can remain dynamically stable while populations and environmental conditions fluctuate within limits.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in stability and change.
solution: Negative feedback, biodiversity and functional redundancy can increase resilience, while strong disturbance may shift a system to another state.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to stability and change.
solution: Complex food webs provide alternative pathways for energy transfer if one population declines.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of stability and change to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Recovery after disturbance depends on intensity, frequency, connectivity, species traits and remaining biological legacies.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will monitor community composition for several years after a disturbance. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: time since disturbance.
Dependent variable: species abundance and diversity.
Controlled variable: sampling method and season.
Expected trend: recovery should show directional change toward a stable composition, though it may not return to the original state.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss stability and change across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
solution: A strong response should: (1) Ecosystems can remain dynamically stable while populations and environmental conditions fluctuate within limits. (2) Negative feedback, biodiversity and functional redundancy can increase resilience, while strong disturbance may shift a system to another state. (3) Complex food webs provide alternative pathways for energy transfer if one population declines. (4) Recovery after disturbance depends on intensity, frequency, connectivity, species traits and remaining biological legacies. (5) Discuss succession, feedback, resilience and tipping points as explanations for both ecosystem stability and ecosystem change.

questions.label: Easy
body: State the central biological principle represented by climate change.
solution:
Current climate change is driven mainly by increased greenhouse-gas concentrations that alter
Earth's energy balance.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain a key mechanism involved in climate change.
solution: Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation; feedbacks such as reduced ice cover can amplify warming.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-function relationship relevant to climate change.
solution: Long-term records, replicated measurements and multiple independent indicators distinguish climate trends from short-term weather variation.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of climate change to predict or explain a biological outcome.
solution: Species may shift ranges or seasonal timing, but responses can be limited by dispersal, habitat fragmentation and ecological interactions.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare flowering date with mean spring temperature across many years. Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one controlled variable, then predict the expected trend.
solution:
Independent variable: mean spring temperature.
Dependent variable: flowering date.
Controlled variable: observation method and species identity.
Expected trend: warmer springs may be associated with earlier flowering, though correlation alone does not prove mechanism.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss climate change across more than one level of biological organization. Include relevant evidence, mechanisms and limitations where appropriate.
ANSWERS AND MARKING POINTS
solution: A strong response should: (1) Current climate change is driven mainly by increased greenhouse-gas concentrations that alter Earth's energy balance. (2) Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation; feedbacks such as reduced ice cover can amplify warming. (3) Long-term records, replicated measurements and multiple independent indicators distinguish climate trends from short-term weather variation. (4) Species may shift ranges or seasonal timing, but responses can be limited by dispersal, habitat fragmentation and ecological interactions. (5) Evaluate evidence, biological impacts, feedbacks, mitigation and adaptation while distinguishing uncertainty from lack of evidence.
